title: The power of the Hypothesis Model when coaching
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton describes a two-day coaching programme in a primary school and uses it to show how Adam Boxer's Hypothesis Model structures lesson observation and feedback. The observer notes specific strengths, forms a single hypothesis about what might improve learning, and gathers critical evidence in the form of a statistic, quote, photo or video. The coaching conversation opens with the teacher's own view of what went well, adds the observer's praise, then presents the hypothesis and evidence and plans one change together. He walks through four lessons and their evidence, and concludes that objective evidence opens the door to change, that one easily implemented strategy beats several, and that coaching only works as part of a continuing programme.
points: A single hypothesis strips out background noise and gives the observer one aspect of teaching to concentrate on.
Concrete evidence such as a count of volunteer versus directed questions, a transcript or a photographed whiteboard makes the issue hard to dispute and prompts the teacher to see it for themselves.
Video is presented as the strongest form of evidence, because it lets teachers watch their lesson free of the demands of teaching it.
Each coaching session should leave the teacher with one rehearsed, implementable action; three or more fails.
A visiting coach has limited impact unless school leaders plan how the coaching will continue after the visit.
quotes: The hypothesis gives a clear focus to the lesson observation. It allows you as an observer to strip out all the background noise and zone in on a single aspect of teaching and learning, considering how it could be improved.
The critical evidence collected is often the key to the success of a coaching session. It is objective, tangible, and unavoidable.

This is the first time I have experimented with video to support my coaching. Obviously, no-one likes being filmed. But I know of no better way to reflect on your own practice than to watch it play out in full, free from all the things that consume your attention in the midst of teaching a lesson.

It is important to choose a single, easily implementable strategy, especially in the first coaching session. We want to give success the best chance of occurring, so we can build upon it going forward. Coaching sessions where the teacher leave with 3 or more things to implement simply do not work.
Out of the 18 questions asked to the class during the time we observed, 16 were directed at volunteers and 2 were directed at students chosen by the teacher. None required all the class to answer.

Coaching like this will only ever work if it is part of a continual programme. The challenge I always present to the member of the leadership team who hires me is to consider how they will keep this going after I leave.
